content: When somebody is hosting a conference or managing a journal where papers come together with Lean projects, what are the best practices for submitting the code? The organizer is worried both about malware and deceptive overriding definitions/notation. Ideally, the submission system should also automatically reject projects that fail build and projects containing Lean files excluded from the build. That said, malware is the main concern. I know that it has been discussed many times before, but I don't know what the current consensus is.

For deception there's comparator, and if you're looking for a "submission system" then lean-eval might be what you're looking for.
For untrusted code (for malware concerns) AFAIK the current solution is to run stuff in a container (e.g. Docker / Podman / etc), and you could also use Kim Morrison's bubble script (also a container under the hood). I believe there's no built-in sandboxing feature (a la Deno or WASM or even seccomp)
If you're running untrusted code, you should sandbox it. That's true for all programming languages.
Is there any system that combines Comparator with Bubble, please?

Great! If the organizer needs to check whether X proves Y, they should run Comparator.

Afterwards, if the organizer wants to make the code accessible for everybody, is there any safe way? Is it even possible to assert that "given code didn't attempt to do anything harmful at compile time" after testing it in a sandbox?

Martin Dvořák said:

If it even possible to assert that "given code didn't attempt to do anything harmful at compile time" after testing it in a sandbox?

The answer is no in general. Sadly! I'll defer to the actual computer scientists for a detailed explanation. (For one, malicious Lean code could detect whether it's run in a sandbox and then "behave", but be malicious when not sandboxed.)

Code can in general attempt to detect that it is part of a sandbox and not execute its malicious behavior until the sandbox is turned off. So if you build again outside of the sandbox thats dangerous. But as long as you just read the text files with an editor that does not try to run lean code, or alternatively work within a VM, you should be fine.
And the fact that we need only compilation to be safe for the target machine doesn't make it easier (i.e., possible) for us?
I can't believe that this problem was not solved many years ago. Lean is not the first programming language. Surely there are precedents here?
The simplest solution is to just use a VM really
Especially at CS conferences just a sandbox for Lean also wouldn't be enough, instructions for artifacts might include running lots of other software that is not naturally sandboxed

Henrik Böving said:

The simplest solution is to just use a VM really

Yes, but future readers who want to browse the code in IDE will also need to use a VM?
If they don't trust the code of course
Are the things that Lean can do at compiletime as dangerous as the things Lean can do at runtime?

This is a read-only solution but people can submit their lean code anonymously using this free service (trusted by oopsla) https://anonymous.4open.science

So you can audit the anonymous solution first and use VMs to clone and build the code.

Every Mathlib PR can be opened in gitpod already using a link, can't it? That seems like the way to go? This way, people who want to look at the contribution don't need to set anything up, just look at a website, and get to have all IDE benefits as well.
Can it be done for projects that aren't PRs?
